A content fingerprint of an R object

Source: R/serialize.R
bin_hash_object.Rd

bin_hash_object() is XXH3 of the body of R's XDR serialisation of x, format version 2 or 3: everything serialize() writes after its header. It is streamed through the hasher, so the serialised bytes are never allocated. Skipping the header, which records the R version that wrote it (and, for version = 3, the native encoding), keeps the digest from changing with those; it stays the same for as long as R writes the same body for x, which R does not promise across its versions (see serialize()), least of all for closures, environments and ALTREP objects. Objects with the same serialisation have the same digest; the converse holds only up to the chance of a collision.

Usage

bin_hash_object(x, algo = c("xxh3_64", "xxh3_128"), version = 2L, seed = 0)

Arguments

x

Any R object.

algo

"xxh3_64" for a 64-bit digest, "xxh3_128" for 128 bits.

version

The serialisation format version, 2 or 3.

seed

A whole number from 0 to 2^53, the XXH3 seed.

Value

A string of 16 or 32 lower-case hexadecimal digits.

Details

It is a fingerprint, not a cryptographic digest and not a durable content address: fast, and well distributed, but not a defence against someone choosing inputs to collide.

The digest is of the bytes R writes, not of the values they stand for, so identical(x, y) does not imply equal digests:

  • A double is its 64 bits. 0 and -0 differ, as do NaNs of different sign or payload, and NA once arithmetic has set its quiet bit (c(NA, 1) + 0), though identical() treats each pair as the same. How NaN and NA propagate through arithmetic depends on the platform (see NA), so the same computation may hash differently on two machines; and on 32-bit x86 even a double NA written as a literal has different bits.

  • A string is its bytes and its encoding mark, so the same non-ASCII text hashes differently when it is marked UTF-8, latin1 or not at all; and unmarked text is in the session's native encoding, which depends on the locale. Apply enc2utf8() to the strings first for a digest that does not depend on either.

Apart from these, the digest of an object is the same on every platform R runs on.

version = 2, the default, writes compact sequences such as 1:10 as the vectors they are; version = 3 writes their compact form, so the same values may then hash differently.

Examples

bin_hash_object(mtcars)
#> [1] "b5864d2491b162b9"
bin_hash_object(mtcars, "xxh3_128")
#> [1] "7999113ed3181597b5864d2491b162b9"
identical(bin_hash_object(1:3 + 0L), bin_hash_object(c(1L, 2L, 3L)))
#> [1] TRUE
